core_principles.text: Stand with feet hip-width apart, keep the back and shoulders straight, and keep the rectus abdominis muscle tight during the lunge.
Take a big step forward and slowly bend both knees until the back knee is just above the floor.

specific_findings.text: In a single-leg lunge, the means of patellar flexion angle at tibiofemoral joint (TFJ) flexion angles of 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°, and 120° were 5.5°, 9.8°, 19.2°, 38.3°, and 64.0°, respectively.

ACL-deficient (ACLD) groups showed significantly increased patellar lateral tilt during almost the entire knee flexion procedure of a single-leg lunge, which was even more pronounced in ACLD knees with medial meniscus deficiency.
The means of patellar lateral tilt angle at TFJ flexion angles of 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°, and 120° were 6.0°, 6.1°, 6.8°, 6.8°, and 8.4°, respectively.
The means of patellar lateral translation at TFJ flexion angles of 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°, and 120° were 8.3, 5.2, 5.6, 6.2, and 6.5 mm, respectively.

core_principles.text: Maintain proper knee alignment during a single-leg lunge to avoid excessive knee valgus, which can alter patellar tracking.
Monitor knee flexion depth during lunges, particularly in individuals with knee injuries, as terminal knee flexion ranges can alter joint translation.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knee to collapse into valgus (inward caving) during the single-leg lunge.

specific_findings.text: Isolated ACLD knees showed significantly reduced internal tibial rotations of about 2–3° compared to ACL-intact knees.
ACLD knees with concomitant medial meniscus deficiency showed significantly increased valgus of about 2–5° compared to other groups.
ACLD knees with concomitant lateral meniscus deficiency showed significantly increased medial tibia translations compared to other groups at 60° of knee flexion.
ACLD knees with combined medial and lateral meniscus deficiency showed significantly increased medial tibia translations at terminal knee flexion ranges of 90–120°.
The study enrolled 60 young subjects to evaluate patellofemoral and tibiofemoral joint kinematics during a single-leg lunge.

consequences.text: An increased knee valgus angle causes the patella to rotate externally, leading to compression between the patella and the femoral trochlear groove.

Altered tibiofemoral joint kinematics lead to abnormal contact locations between the patella and the femur, which can cause adverse patellofemoral joint outcomes and subsequent cartilage degeneration.
